questions.stem: Why is the gas identity irrelevant when converting volume to moles at fixed conditions?

options.explanation: Most laboratory gases are compounds.

options.text: Because volume never depends on temperature
options.explanation: Volume responds strongly to temperature.

options.text: Equal volumes of any gases contain equal numbers of particles under the same conditions
options.explanation: Avogadro's law makes the volume-per-mole universal.

options.text: Because all gases have identical molar masses
options.explanation: Molar masses differ; the volume law does not depend on them.

options.explanation: Each propane volume gives 3 + 4 = 7 volumes of gaseous product: 6.50 x 7 = 45.5 dm^3.

questions.stem: State the molar gas volumes at r.t.p. and s.t.p. with their condition definitions.
questions.modelAnswer: At r.t.p. (293 K / 20 degrees C, 101.3 kPa) the molar gas volume is 24.0 dm^3; at s.t.p. (273 K / 0 degrees C, 101.3 kPa) it is 22.4 dm^3.

questions.stem: State the equation linking moles of gas to its volume at fixed conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles of gas = volume of gas in dm^3 / molar gas volume in dm^3.

questions.stem: Explain why gas volumes can pass straight through an equation's ratio while masses cannot.
questions.modelAnswer: At fixed temperature and pressure, equal volumes contain equal numbers of gas particles, so a volume ratio between gases IS a mole ratio; masses require conversion through each substance's molar mass because a gram of one gas is not a gram's worth of formula units of another.

questions.stem: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, at s.t.p., released when 1.50 g of sodium reacts fully with water, quoting every step.
questions.modelAnswer: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; n(Na) = 1.50 / 23.0 = 0.0652 mol; ratio 2:1 gives 0.0326 mol H2; V = 0.0326 mol on 22.4 dm^3 per mol gives 0.730 dm^3 (3 s.f.).

questions.stem: Which unit set does the ideal gas expression pV = nRT demand?

options.explanation: Volume must be m^3, not cm^3.

options.text: Pa, m^3, mol, K with R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1
options.explanation: Those are the SI pairings the gas constant is calibrated for.

options.text: kPa, dm^3, mol, degrees C with R = 8.31
options.explanation: Those mixed units contradict the constant's calibration.
Another non-SI blend requiring different R.

questions.stem: What are the kinetic theory's core assumptions?

options.text: Fixed particle volume and inelastic collisions
options.explanation: Both violate the ideal assumptions.
Temperature is one consequence; the assumption list is longer.

options.text: Fast random motion, negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions
options.explanation: Those four assumptions define the ideal gas model.

options.text: Heavy particles, strong attractions, slow motion
options.explanation: That is the opposite of the model.

questions.stem: Why does the ideal gas equation still serve real gases well in exam calculations?

options.explanation: Units are precisely where marks live.

options.text: Real gases come very close to ideal behaviour under ordinary conditions
options.explanation: Deviations shrink at low pressure and moderate temperature, so the model predicts well.

options.text: Because real gases have no intermolecular forces at all
options.explanation: They do; the forces are just small enough to neglect.

options.text: Because R is re-measured for each gas
options.explanation: R is universal.

questions.stem: State the ideal gas equation with every variable's unit.
questions.modelAnswer: pV = nRT with pressure in Pa, volume in m^3, n in mol, R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1 and temperature in K.

questions.stem: State the three unit conversions pV = nRT calculations typically need.
questions.modelAnswer: kPa to Pa multiply by 1000; cm^3 to m^3 multiply by 10^-6; Celsius to Kelvin add 273.

questions.stem: Explain why temperature must enter in Kelvin, not Celsius.
questions.modelAnswer: The equation tracks average kinetic energy, which starts from absolute zero - the total cessation of particle motion; Celsius zero is an arbitrary ice point, so using it would treat a 273 K energy floor as if it were nothing, collapsing the proportionality.
